n: God gives Jonah a second chance, with the same call. The Lord is patient with His servants.

f.g: A comforting reminder that God offers second chances.

n: “Go to Nineveh and preach what I tell you.” This time Jonah must deliver God’s message, not his own.

f.w: the preaching that I bid thee

n: This time Jonah obeys. Nineveh was so large that it took three days to visit or cross the whole area.

f.g: May describe the city with its suburbs, or the time to make a full round of visits.

n: After a day’s walk into the city, Jonah announces: “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” In Hebrew it is only five words — a short, bare sermon.

f.g: Forty is often a period of testing or preparation in scripture.
Hebrew haphak — the word used of Sodom’s overthrow; it can also mean “turned around,” which is what happened through repentance.

n: Amazingly, the Ninevites believe God. Everyone, from greatest to least, fasts and wears sackcloth. Jesus later held them up as an example of repentance.

f.w: the people of Nineveh believed God

f.g: Rough cloth worn in mourning and repentance.

n: The king himself steps down from his throne, removes his royal robe, and sits in ashes in humility.
The king decrees a total fast — even the animals may not eat or drink.

f.g: Including animals in mourning rituals was a known custom in the ancient world.

n: Everyone must cry mightily to God and turn from evil and violence. True repentance means changing behavior, not just rituals.

f.w: turn every one from his evil way

f.g: Assyria was notorious for cruelty in war.

n: “Who knows? Maybe God will relent and we won’t perish.” They hope in God’s mercy without presuming on it.
God sees their changed actions and relents from the disaster He had announced. His warnings are invitations; repentance changes outcomes.

f.g: Changed His mind about the disaster — not that God had done wrong.
